question: A 3-year-old boy was brought in by his parents for undescended testes. The physical examination showed an absence of the left testis in the scrotum. Inguinal swelling was noted on the left side and was surgically corrected. Which of the following conditions will most likely occur in the later stages of his life?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Undescended testis -> Increased risk of testicular cancer -> 80% CHAIN: Surgical correction of undescended testis -> Decreased risk of testicular cancer -> 70% CHAIN: Inguinal swelling -> Surgical correction -> Decreased risk of torsion testis -> 60% CHAIN: Absence of left testis in scrotum -> Increased risk of spermatocele on the contralateral side -> 50% CHAIN: Inguinal swelling -> Surgical correction -> Decreased risk of epididymitis -> 80%
enhanced_information: The surgical correction of undescended testis decreases the risk of testicular cancer. Inguinal swelling, when surgically corrected, reduces the risk of torsion testis and epididymitis. The absence of the left testis in the scrotum may increase the risk of spermatocele on the contralateral side. The presence of a spermatocele on ultrasonography does not directly correlate with the later development of testicular cancer.
analysis: The core medical principle is that the surgical correction of undescended testis reduces the risk of testicular cancer. In this case, the absence of the left testis in the scrotum may increase the risk of spermatocele on the contralateral side. While the presence of a spermatocele does not directly correlate with testicular cancer, the increased risk of spermatocele is a potential long-term consequence. Therefore, the most likely condition to occur in the later stages of his life is spermatocele.
